y1: Joseph receives a message in a dream again and leaves that very night. Just like in the first chapter, Joseph obeys not with words, but with actions.
y2: Egypt was a place where Israelites had taken refuge during hard times since ancient days. At that time, there was also a large Jewish community in Alexandria.
y3: Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1: “I called my son out of Egypt.” Originally, this referred to Israel's Exodus. Matthew shows that Jesus is reliving the history of Israel and obeying perfectly where Israel failed.
y5: Herod ordered the killing of all boys in and around Bethlehem who were two years old and under. Since it was a small village, it is thought that about ten children died, but every child was their family's whole world.
y6: Matthew quotes the words of the prophet Jeremiah: “Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted.”
y7: Matthew does not try to sugarcoat this tragedy. The Bible is a book that weeps with us in the face of suffering. But Jeremiah 31 promises a “new covenant” and restoration in the very same chapter. Even in the midst of tears, God's story does not end.
y9: After Herod dies, an angel appears in a dream again and tells him to return to Israel. But Herod's cruel son Archelaus was ruling in Judea.
y10: When Joseph was afraid, God guided him to Galilee through another dream. In Matthew chapters 1–2 alone, God guides through dreams five times.
y12: Joseph's family settles in a small village in Galilee called Nazareth. It was an ordinary village with only a few hundred people.
y13: The saying, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” shows that Nazareth was despised. Jesus grew up in such a place.
y14: This exact sentence is not written in the Old Testament. Many scholars explain it as a wordplay on the word “branch” (Hebrew netser) in Isaiah 11:1 and a reference to the despised Messiah (Isaiah 53).
verse: “He arose and took the young child and his mother by night, and departed into Egypt.”
prayer: Lord God, I praise Jesus, who became a refugee and came to the lowest place. Help me to believe that Your story does not end, even in the midst of suffering and tears. Help me to be a person who obeys as soon as I hear, just like Joseph. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Amen.
d0: obey. It literally means “to listen under.” It means to act according to the words you hear. Joseph doesn't speak a single word in chapters 1–2, but he obeys immediately after every dream.
d1: Exodus. In the time of Moses, God saved Israel from slavery in Egypt. This is the main picture of salvation. Jesus being tested in the wilderness for 40 days in chapter 4 is connected to Israel's 40 years in the wilderness.
d2: Jeremiah. A prophet who lived during the Babylonian exile. He is called the “weeping prophet” because he cried a lot seeing the destruction of his nation. Jeremiah chapter 31 also contains God's promise of the “new covenant.”
d3: Rachel. She was Jacob's most beloved wife and was buried on the way to Bethlehem. She is a symbol of the mothers of Israel. Rachel's tomb is still at the entrance to Bethlehem today.
d4: Archelaus. He ruled Judea after his father died, but he was so cruel that Rome eventually banished him. It is recorded that he killed three thousand people in the temple when he came to power.
d5: Nazareth. It was a small, unknown village that was never even mentioned in the Old Testament. Jesus' followers were once called the “sect of the Nazarenes” (Acts 24:5).
